title: Science teaching self-reflection | Bring one idea back into the next lesson

qcReview.basis: The 4 English item texts and order match the corresponding factor in Kang et al. Appendix B, pp. 510–513. The original study used five frequency positions; methods §3.1 lists only endpoints 1 = rarely and 5 = always. The project preserves numeric 2–4 and the complete-response 1–5 factor mean. No study averages, norms or thresholds are used. The item count follows Appendix B and Table 4; Table 7 reports conflicting counts and is not used as evidence for this report.

interpretations.scoreLabel: Reflection, feedback and professional learning (descriptive mean, 1–5)
interpretations.headline: Bring one idea back into the next lesson
interpretations.summary:
After a workshop, a teacher tries one prompt for collecting students’ first ideas. A few students say the prompt is easier to use after seeing an example. The teacher changes it and tries it again. A short workshop idea becomes a tool the teacher can improve through ordinary classroom work.

This average reflects the ways you report reviewing lessons, using student feedback, applying professional learning and noticing changes that may matter to the science curriculum. The paper calls this group the ‘traditional mode’. Its practices can still help you turn an impression or a course idea into a deliberate change.

guidance.text: Choose one point from a course, conversation or lesson review. Name the activity where you will try it. Collect one piece of student feedback that can tell you how to adapt it.
After the lesson, write what you tried, what was different for learners, and which part you would keep. Bring that example to a colleague if you want another perspective.

limitations: Kang, N.-H., Kang, H., Maeng, S., Park, J., & Jeong, E. (2020). Teacher Competency in Competency-Focused Science Teaching in the South Korean Context: Teacher Self-Assessment Instrument Development and Application. Asia-Pacific Science Education, 6(2), 480–513. https://doi.org/10.1163/23641177-BJA10012 (CC BY 4.0, https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/). The project separates each published factor and supplies its own instructions, complete-answer rule and feedback.

This score is the mean of 4 responses, from 1 (rarely) to 5 (always), and requires all 4 answers. It describes self-reported practices and may include judgments about your understanding or effectiveness. It contains no objective performance score, norm, or cross-factor total.

The original study used the full instrument with 210 South Korean primary and secondary science teachers. This research and self-reflection version uses the published English item wording. The project has not obtained the Korean administration form. Separate use of this factor and equivalence to a Chinese version have not been established.
report.disclaimer: For your own professional learning and research reflection as a science teacher. The result supports a conversation about practice and does not establish teaching quality, teacher eligibility, or student outcomes.
